article.abstract: A randomized trial in Italy included 302 adults for analysis: 151 in the compound 111 group and 151 in the placebo group; all were adults with metabolic syndrome. article.title: Psyllium added to breakfast and fasting cholesterol in adults with prediabetes
article.abstract: Soluble viscous fibre may alter lipid absorption, but its usefulness alongside routine dietary advice remains uncertain in people with early disturbances of glucose regulation. We examined whether taking psyllium with breakfast lowered fasting low-density lipoprotein cholesterol without requiring a wider change in food choices. In a parallel randomized trial at two clinics in Portugal, the analysis included 126 adults with prediabetes: 63 received psyllium and 63 received a cellulose placebo. Participants consumed 8 g daily for 10 weeks; fasting cholesterol at week 10 was compared between groups with adjustment for baseline cholesterol. Both groups received the same brief dietary advice, and lipid-lowering prescriptions were kept stable throughout follow-up. Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol was lower with psyllium than placebo by 0.24 mmol/L (95% CI -0.39 to -0.09; p=0.002). Body weight changed by -0.6 kg with psyllium and -0.4 kg with placebo, whereas fasting glucose differed by only -0.08 mmol/L between groups (p=0.47). Mild bloating was recorded by nine psyllium recipients and four placebo recipients, with no participant stopping treatment for this reason. A modest cholesterol benefit accompanied this simple breakfast supplement, although the short observation period does not establish whether the difference persists or reduces cardiovascular events.

article.title: An evening fibre supplement during community cholesterol management
article.abstract: Keeping a soluble fibre supplement in an ordinary evening routine may be easier than replacing several foods at once, yet adherence and lipid responses can vary considerably. This community study tested psyllium against a matched cellulose preparation in adults with prediabetes who had not recently changed medication. A randomized parallel trial recruited adults with prediabetes from community health services; 79 were assigned to psyllium and the remaining recruits received cellulose placebo. The supplements were supplied in indistinguishable sachets, and participants were asked to mix them with a familiar drink rather than change their usual meals. Dietitians gave identical written advice, while unused sachets and brief telephone interviews were used to assess adherence. Fasting low-density lipoprotein cholesterol was lower among psyllium recipients than among those allocated cellulose placebo, with the direction of the difference consistent across participating practices. Mean systolic pressure fell by 2.1 mmHg in the fibre group and 1.7 mmHg among placebo recipients; the between-arm pressure contrast was not significant (P = .71). Median sachet use was 88% [interquartile range 76–95], and no serious digestive event was reported. Adding psyllium was associated with a small improvement in cholesterol under everyday conditions, but longer observation and a broader patient population would be needed before drawing conclusions about sustained benefit.

article.title: Sitagliptin and fasting triglycerides during stable diabetes care
article.abstract: Lipid changes during glucose-lowering treatment are often secondary observations, and their size can depend on changes in diet or other prescriptions. We evaluated fasting triglycerides as a prespecified secondary outcome of adding sitagliptin, an incretin-based medicine, to otherwise stable treatment in adults with type 2 diabetes. The double-blind randomized trial compared sitagliptin and matching placebo in adults with type 2 diabetes, with every randomized participant included in the endpoint analysis. Treatment continued for 18 weeks, and fasting triglycerides were assessed at week 18 alongside the prespecified glycaemic outcomes; laboratory staff remained unaware of treatment allocation. Glucose-lowering and lipid-lowering background therapies were held constant, and participants were asked to maintain their usual physical activity. Sitagliptin produced a statistically significant reduction in triglycerides relative to placebo: the mean difference was -0.16 mmol/L, with a 95% confidence interval of -0.29 to -0.03. Glycated haemoglobin was lower by 0.48 percentage points (p < 0.001), while the between-group difference in body weight was -0.2 kg (p = 0.62). Symptomatic hypoglycaemia occurred in three treated participants and two placebo recipients, and no serious event was considered treatment related. The modest triglyceride reduction accompanied improved glycaemia in this sample, but the study was not designed to determine whether either change translated into fewer vascular events.

article.title: Triglyceride response to additional sitagliptin in outpatient diabetes clinics
article.abstract: Whether a glucose-lowering agent also improves triglyceride concentrations is clinically relevant when weight and background lipid therapy remain stable. We therefore included a lipid assessment in an outpatient comparison of the incretin-based medicine sitagliptin and placebo, with the analysis specified before treatment allocation was revealed. The randomized, masked study recruited adults with type 2 diabetes through outpatient appointments, using indistinguishable treatment packs to conceal the assigned medication from participants and staff. Mean fasting triglyceride concentrations were compared between the allocated groups; the laboratory received coded records, and the investigators checked the consistency of measurement procedures before reviewing the results. Participants continued their usual medications and received no weight-loss programme; drug adherence was assessed from returned tablets. No difference in triglycerides was detected between sitagliptin and placebo (P=.74), despite the direction of the glycaemic response favouring active treatment. Despite this lipid finding, glycated haemoglobin declined by an additional 0.44 percentage points with sitagliptin (P<.001), and mean weight changes were -0.1 and 0.0 kg respectively. Treatment discontinuation was uncommon, involving four participants on sitagliptin and five on placebo, usually because they no longer wished to continue taking the study tablets. Improved glycaemic control did not coincide with a detectable triglyceride benefit in this setting; a larger study would be required to distinguish a very small lipid effect from no effect.

article.title: Ferritin and fasting glucose across a community metabolic syndrome sample
article.abstract: Ferritin is an iron-storage protein with links to inflammatory activity, making its metabolic interpretation dependent on the population in which it is measured. We studied the relation between ferritin and fasting glucose in adults with metabolic syndrome, without using ferritin to define eligibility. This cross-sectional investigation involved adults with metabolic syndrome attending community clinics in Spain; the analysis used the complete clinical records available from the participating patients. Linear regression examined the ferritin–glucose relation, while the laboratory team processed coded specimens without access to the clinical questionnaire responses or the investigators’ working hypothesis. People taking iron supplements or receiving treatment for anaemia were excluded, and instructions about fasting were provided during booking rather than left to participants to interpret. Higher ferritin was associated with higher fasting glucose in the metabolic syndrome sample, a positive relation that remained the principal finding of the exploratory clinical assessment. Median ferritin was 146 micrograms/L [interquartile range 91–214], and its correlation with C-reactive protein was modest (r=0.24; p=0.001). Women and men showed associations in the same direction, with no evidence of a sex interaction (p=0.58). Higher ferritin accompanied higher fasting glucose in this metabolic syndrome sample, although the cross-sectional design cannot establish sequence or separate iron storage from residual inflammatory influences.

article.title: Ferritin and glucose among endurance athletes with depleted iron stores
article.abstract: Metabolic associations derived from clinic populations may not transfer to highly active people whose iron stores are low, even when the same laboratory measurements are used. An athlete screening programme provided an opportunity to examine ferritin and fasting glucose in that contrasting physiological setting. We conducted a cross-sectional study of adult endurance athletes with depleted iron stores, recruiting through sports health assessments rather than clinics treating metabolic disease. The relation of ferritin to fasting glucose was examined by linear regression, with laboratory personnel kept unaware of training history until the measurements had been completed. Participants were training regularly, had no metabolic syndrome, and had not yet begun iron replacement; recent infection was an exclusion criterion. The ferritin–glucose association was negative: athletes with higher ferritin had lower fasting glucose within this iron-depleted population. Ferritin had a median of 18 micrograms/L [IQR 12–24], while a separate analysis found no clear association with resting heart rate (p=0.39). Weekly running time averaged 6.3 ± 2.1 hours, and women and men had similar glucose associations (interaction p=0.66). Within this iron-depleted athletic population, higher ferritin accompanied slightly lower glucose; the observation does not show that increasing iron stores would lower glucose or justify supplementation for metabolic purposes.
